items.title: fix: pin trivy-action to SHA (security hardening)
items.body:
## What

Pin `aquasecurity/trivy-action` from `@master` to the commit SHA for v0.34.1 (`e368e328979b113139d6f9068e03accaed98a518`).

## Why

On 28 February 2026, the [aquasecurity/trivy](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy) repository was compromised as part of the [hackerbot-claw GitHub Actions exploitation campaign](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-exploitation-campaign). The attacker gained full control of the repo via a stolen PAT, renamed the default branch, deleted all releases, and pushed a malicious VS Code extension.

Referencing `trivy-action@master` means our workflow pulls whatever code is on the `master` branch at run time. During the compromise window, this could have meant executing attacker-controlled code with access to this repo's secrets and a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

SHA pinning is immune to this class of attack because commit hashes are immutable — even if the repo is fully compromised, an attacker cannot change what a SHA resolves to.

## Additional notes

- This is part of an org-wide security hardening effort following the hackerbot-claw incident

items.title: Add explicit permissions to GitHub Actions workflows
items.body:
## Context

Neither `build-validation.yml` nor `release.yml` declares a `permissions:` block. Without one, workflows inherit the repo/org default — which is typically `write` for all scopes. This means even a read-only CI job like build validation runs with a token that could push commits, merge PRs, or modify releases.

The hackerbot-claw campaign (Feb–Mar 2026) demonstrated the real-world impact: exfiltrated `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `contents: write` allowed the attacker to push malicious commits, delete releases, and rename the trivy repository.

Related: PR #80 (SHA pinning + persist-credentials), issue #81 (Dependabot), issue #82 (zizmor).

## Proposed changes

### `build-validation.yml`
Add top-level read-only permissions (this workflow only reads code, lints, builds, and runs tests):

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
```

### `release.yml`
Add scoped write permissions (needs to create GitHub releases):

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: write
```

## Why this matters

Least-privilege tokens limit blast radius. Even if an attacker achieves code execution inside a CI runner, a read-only token can't push commits, merge PRs, or create releases. This is the single lowest-effort, highest-value GHA hardening step.

## Notes

- DataDog deployed this exact fix within 9 hours of the hackerbot-claw attack (PR DataDog/datadog-iac-scanner#9)
- This pairs well with `persist-credentials: false` (already in PR #80)
- zizmor (issue #82) can enforce this going forward

items.body:
## Problem

Fullsend generates GitHub Actions workflows programmatically — the shim workflow (`internal/layers/enrollment.go`) and agent dispatch workflow (`internal/layers/workflows.go`) are Go string constants that get written to target repos and `.fullsend` during `admin install`. These generated workflows are security-critical: they handle secrets, cross-repo dispatch, and agent execution.

Currently, actionlint runs as a pre-commit hook on standalone `.github/workflows/*.yml` files, but it does **not** validate the workflow YAML embedded in Go string constants. A syntax error, expression injection, or permission misconfiguration in these templates would not be caught until the workflow is deployed to a live repo.

## Proposal

Add workflow security scanning at three layers:

### 1. Go test-time validation (actionlint as Go library)

actionlint is already used in pre-commit and is importable as `github.com/rhysd/actionlint`. Add a test that parses and lints all generated workflow string constants:

```go
// internal/layers/workflows_lint_test.go
func TestGeneratedWorkflows_Lint(t *testing.T) {
    workflows := map[string]string{
        "agent.yaml":   agentWorkflowContent,
        "fullsend.yaml": (&EnrollmentLayer{org: "test-org"}).shimWorkflowContent(),
    }
    for name, content := range workflows {
        l, err := actionlint.NewLinter(io.Discard, &actionlint.LinterOptions{})
        require.NoError(t, err)
        errs, err := l.Lint(name, []byte(content), nil)
        require.NoError(t, err)
        assert.Empty(t, errs, "generated workflow %s has lint errors", name)
    }
}
```

This catches syntax errors, type mismatches, invalid action inputs, and script injection at `go test` time — before any deployment.

### 2. Security-focused scanning in CI (zizmor or fluxgate)

actionlint's only security check is script injection detection. Security-specific scanners catch vulnerability classes actionlint does not:

| Vulnerability | actionlint | [zizmor](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) | [fluxgate](https://github.com/north-echo/fluxgate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expression injection | Yes (`expression`) | Yes (`template-injection`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-002) |
| Pwn request | No | Partial (`dangerous-triggers` flags trigger, no execution analysis) | Yes (FG-001, with post-checkout execution + mitigation analysis) |
| Unpinned actions | No | Yes (`unpinned-uses`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-003) |
| Overly broad permissions | No (syntax only) | Yes (`excessive-permissions`) | Yes (FG-004) |
| Cache poisoning | No | Yes (`cache-poisoning`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-010) |
| Self-hosted + external triggers | No | Yes (`self-hosted-runner`) | Yes (FG-009) |
| OIDC misconfiguration | No | No | Yes (FG-008) |
| Bot actor TOCTOU | No | Yes (`bot-conditions`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-011) |
| Known vulnerable actions | No | Yes (`known-vulnerable-actions`, auto-fix) | No |
| Credential persistence in artifacts | No | Yes (`artipacked`, auto-fix) | No |
| `contains()` substring bypass | No | Yes (`unsound-contains`) | No |
| GITHUB_ENV/PATH writes | No | Yes (`github-env`) | No |
| Secrets in logs | No | Yes (`unredacted-secrets`) | Yes (FG-005) |

**Candidates:**

- **[zizmor](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor)** (Rust, 4k stars, Trail of Bits) — 34 rules, auto-fix for 14, SARIF/JSON/GitHub output. Gold standard for GHA security scanning. Deployed by Grafana Labs across 2,000+ repos. CLI integration from Go via subprocess.
- **[fluxgate](https://github.com/north-echo/fluxgate)** (Go, very new) — 19 rules across GHA/GitLab/Azure. Strongest pwn request detection (post-checkout execution analysis with mitigation modeling). Built in response to the hackerbot-claw campaign. CLI integration only (packages under `internal/`, not importable as Go library).

Add a CI step that extracts generated workflow YAML and scans it:

```yaml
- name: Scan generated workflows
  run: |
    go test -run TestExtractWorkflows ./internal/layers/ -extract-dir /tmp/workflows
    zizmor --format sarif /tmp/workflows/
```

### 3. `workflow_dispatch` input injection (branch `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6`)

The unmerged `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6` branch switches from `workflow_call` to `workflow_dispatch`. The shim in target repos dispatches to `.fullsend` via `gh workflow run`, passing event data as `workflow_dispatch` inputs. This introduces a distinct attack surface:

The v6 shim passes `toJSON(github.event)` as the `event_payload` input, which includes user-supplied content (issue bodies, PR titles, comment text). If the receiving `agent.yaml` interpolates these inputs into `run:` blocks via `${{ inputs.event_payload }}`, it is vulnerable to expression injection — the same class as `${{ github.event.issue.body }}` but arriving through a different path.

**Scanner coverage for `workflow_dispatch` input injection:**

| Tool | Detects dispatch input injection? | Details |
|---|---|---|
| actionlint | Yes | Flags untrusted `${{ }}` expressions in `run:` blocks, including `inputs.*` |
| zizmor (`template-injection`) | Yes | Covers `workflow_dispatch` inputs as injection sinks |
| fluxgate (FG-002) | Yes | Explicitly covers dispatch inputs and reusable workflow inputs |

All three scanners would catch `${{ inputs.event_payload }}` in a `run:` block. However, setting it as an **env var** (`EVENT_PAYLOAD: ${{ inputs.event_payload }}`) is treated differently — the value is passed through the runner's environment, not shell-interpolated, so it is not directly injectable via shell metacharacters. The risk shifts to how downstream code reads and uses that env var.

**Mitigation:** Pass only structured reference fields (repo name, issue number, event type) instead of raw event payloads. The agent fetches full context via the GitHub API using its own App credentials at runtime.

### 4. Runtime protection in generated workflows (Harden-Runner)

Inject [step-security/harden-runner](https://github.com/step-security/harden-runner) as the first step in all generated agent dispatch workflows. This provides runtime monitoring (network egress, file integrity, process activity) that catches supply chain compromise and credential exfiltration during execution — things static analysis cannot detect.

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: step-security/harden-runner@<pinned-sha>
    with:
      egress-policy: audit
```

Harden-Runner has detected real-world supply chain attacks including tj-actions/changed-files (CVE-2025-30066), NX build system, and the hackerbot-claw campaign in CNCF Backstage.

## Why this matters for fullsend specifically

Fullsend generates workflows that:
- Pass secrets cross-repo (App PEM keys via `workflow_call`)
- Handle user-supplied event data (issue bodies, PR descriptions, comments)
- Run on repos the fullsend operator does not control (enrolled target repos)
- Will eventually execute LLM-driven agents with write access to production repos

A vulnerability in a generated workflow template affects **every enrolled repo** simultaneously — the blast radius is the entire fullsend installation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] actionlint Go library validates all generated workflow string constants in `go test`
- [ ] CI pipeline includes security-focused scanning (zizmor or fluxgate) on generated workflows
- [ ] Generated agent dispatch workflows include Harden-Runner as first step
- [ ] Action references in generated workflows use SHA pinning (not mutable tags like `@v4`)
- [ ] Generated workflows set minimum required `permissions:` (not defaults)
- [ ] `workflow_dispatch` inputs (if adopted from `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6`) pass only structured reference fields, not raw event payloads

## References

- [Unpacking Security Scanners for GitHub Actions Workflows](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.14455v1) — no single scanner covers all vulnerability classes
- [GitHub Security Lab: Preventing pwn requests](https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/)
- [Upwind: hackerbot-claw campaign](https://www.upwind.io/feed/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-pull-request-rce) — autonomous bot exploiting `pull_request_target` at scale
- Story 7: Agent Sandbox & Action Constraints (#130)
- Story 6: Prompt Injection Defense (#129)

items.title: chore(ci): merge all Dependabot updates after CI passes
items.body:
Auto-merge every Dependabot update, including major and security updates, only after CI is green for the exact commit being merged. The repositories do not currently enforce CI checks as merge requirements, so simply enabling GitHub auto-merge would allow merges before CI finishes.

The workflow checks the latest Actions runs, check runs, and legacy commit statuses. Pending, failed, cancelled, or absent checks leave the PR open. Neutral/skipped checks may accompany successful CI, but at least one successful check is required. It approves and squash-merges only open, non-draft Dependabot PRs from this repository, revalidates the current head, and uses the merge API's SHA guard. Existing review/merge protections remain authoritative.

CI completion triggers the check; external check/status events and an hourly retry cover checks that finish last. The workflow never checks out or executes PR code, ignores its own obsolete automation checks, and continues the retry sweep after individual PR failures. Manual dispatch defaults to a read-only preview. The reviewer-request workflow is removed.

**Activation requirement:** configure a maintenance GitHub App/PAT credential as the `DEPENDABOT_AUTOMERGE_TOKEN` Actions secret (or update the reference to the existing organization credential). It needs Actions/checks/statuses read and contents/pull-requests write for these repositories. The built-in token is read-only and may only serve preview/read operations; it cannot perform merges. A separate credential is necessary so the merge still triggers normal push-based deployment and post-merge CI. This PR remains a draft while that credential is unresolved. Never add this CI-only credential to application environments or Compose.

Validation: 55 behavior tests execute the exact inline script shipped in the workflow; workflow lint and Station's Biome check pass. Cases cover failed/pending/no checks, major updates, stale heads, forks, pagination, reruns, merge protections, credential absence, dry runs, external-check retries, and a blocked PR followed by a mergeable PR in the same sweep. Real API read-only checks are recorded separately; no dependency PR was approved or merged during validation.

The standing DefangLabs webhook watch already observes ordinary Actions CI failures on any branch; this PR leaves that routing intact.

Constitution: security and simplicity pass (no untrusted checkout, minimal token scopes, exact-SHA merge, native protections preserved); product DX, multi-cloud and cloud resource gates are not applicable.

- [x] This PR adds or changes no user-facing copy

References: [GITHUB_TOKEN event suppression](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow#triggering-a-workflow-from-a-workflow), [workflow completion and trigger rules](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_run).

items.body:
## Summary

Several workflows don't declare explicit `permissions:` blocks and inherit the repository default. If the repo default is `write-all` (GitHub's default for older repos), these workflows run with unnecessary write access to contents, packages, deployments, etc.

**Affected workflows:**
- `check-links.yml` — only needs `contents: read`
- `playwright.yml` — only needs `contents: read`
- `unit-tests.yml` — only needs `contents: read`
- `release.yml` — needs `contents: write` for creating releases, but should declare it explicitly
- `require-release-label.yml` — only needs `pull-requests: read`

## Why this matters

The [hackerbot-claw campaign](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-exploitation) demonstrated how over-permissioned `GITHUB_TOKEN`s amplify the blast radius of CI/CD attacks. In the awesome-go attack, a token with `contents: write` + `pull-requests: write` was exfiltrated and could have been used to push malicious commits.

Setting explicit least-privilege permissions on every workflow is a defense-in-depth measure — even if a workflow is otherwise safe, an explicit `permissions` block limits what a compromised action or injected command could do with the token.

## Recommended fix

Add a top-level `permissions:` block to each workflow scoped to the minimum needed. For most of these, that's just `contents: read`.

## Context

Related to #1032 (zizmor auditor would flag this going forward) and the broader supply chain hardening effort (#1031, #1030).

items.title: security: GitHub Actions 全リポジトリ セキュリティ強化 (2026-03-03)
items.body:
## 背景

hackerbot-claw による GitHub Actions 攻撃キャンペーン ([StepSecurity 詳報](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-exploitation)) を受け、xxVet シリーズ全リポジトリの CI/CD ワークフローをセキュリティ強化した。

### 攻撃手法と xxVet の対応状況

| 手法 | 内容 | xxVet 対応 |
|---|---|---|
| Pwn Request | `pull_request_target` + fork checkout | ✅ 元々 `pull_request` のみ |
| スラッシュコマンド認可漏れ | author_association チェックなし | ✅ 該当なし |
| ブランチ名インジェクション | 非エスケープ `${{ }}` を bash 展開 | ✅ 該当なし |
| 直接スクリプト注入 | fork PR でのスクリプト改ざん | ✅ pull_request で権限制限済み |
| AI レビュアー操作 | 悪意コードを AI に approve させる | ✅ 未設定 |

---

## 実施した変更

### 対応済みリポジトリ (8件)

| リポジトリ | 変更内容 |
|---|---|
| agentvet | SHA固定 + `permissions: contents: read` + `--provenance` |
| ApiVet | SHA固定 + permissions + --provenance |
| DockerVet | SHA固定 + permissions + `dockervet@0.1.0` 固定 (was `@latest`) + --provenance |
| ExtVet | SHA固定 + permissions + --provenance |
| ModelVet | SHA固定 (v6系) + permissions + --provenance |
| GeoVet | SHA固定 + permissions + --provenance |
| SecretVet | SHA固定 + permissions + CI/publish ワークフロー新規追加 |
| 3-shake/SpecVet | SHA固定 + permissions |

### 変更の具体内容

#### 1. Action バージョンを SHA ピン化

```yaml
# Before
uses: actions/checkout@v4

# After
uses: actions/checkout@34e114876b0b11c390a56381ad16ebd13914f8d5  # v4
```

固定した SHA 一覧:

| Action | タグ | SHA |
|---|---|---|
| actions/checkout | v4 | `34e114876b0b11c390a56381ad16ebd13914f8d5` |
| actions/checkout | v6 | `de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd` |
| actions/setup-node | v4 | `49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020` |
| actions/setup-node | v6 | `6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238` |
| github/codeql-action/upload-sarif | v3 | `ae9ef3a1d2e3413523c3741725c30064970cc0d4` |
| softprops/action-gh-release | v1 | `de2c0eb89ae2a093876385947365aca7b0e5f844` |
| softprops/action-gh-release | v2 | `a06a81a03ee405af7f2048a818ed3f03bbf83c7b` |
| actions/upload-artifact | v4 | `ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02` |

#### 2. permissions ブロック追加

```yaml
# 全ワークフロー共通
permissions:
  contents: read   # デフォルト全書き込み → 読み取りのみに制限

# SARIF upload ジョブのみ
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write

# npm publish ジョブのみ
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write   # npm provenance 用
```

#### 3. npm publish に --provenance 追加

```yaml
run: npm publish --access public --provenance
```

SBOM に署名が入り、サプライチェーン攻撃への耐性向上。

#### 4. dockervet@latest → バージョン固定 (DockerVet のみ)

```yaml
# Before (危険: 実行時に解決 = npmパッケージ侵害で全リポジトリが踏み台になる)
npx --yes dockervet@latest

# After
npx --yes dockervet@0.1.0
```

items.title: Dangerous Workflow: some user input are not being detected as untrusted input.
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
The current Dangerous Workflow check looks for places where untrusted user inputs could be used for Script Injection, such as:
```
- name: Check title
  run: |
    title="${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
    if [[ ! $title =~ ^.*:\ .*$ ]]; then
      echo "Bad issue title"
      exit 1
    fi
```

The problem is that Scorecard is not considering the whole range of user input that might lead to Script Injection. The [piece of code](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/70d045b9ef00e7171ce3950aca38eef6ea4d7308/checks/raw/dangerous_workflow.go#L30-L56) that lists the user inputs is the following:

```
func containsUntrustedContextPattern(variable string) bool {
        // GitHub event context details that may be attacker controlled.
        // See https://securitylab.github.com/research/github-actions-untrusted-input/
        untrustedContextPattern := regexp.MustCompile(
                `.*(issue\.title|` +
                        `issue\.body|` +
                        `pull_request\.title|` +
                        `pull_request\.body|` +
                        `comment\.body|` +
                        `review\.body|` +
                        `review_comment\.body|` +
                        `pages.*\.page_name|` +
                        `commits.*\.message|` +
                        `head_commit\.message|` +
                        `head_commit\.author\.email|` +
                        `head_commit\.author\.name|` +
                        `commits.*\.author\.email|` +
                        `commits.*\.author\.name|` +
                        `pull_request\.head\.ref|` +
                        `pull_request\.head\.label|` +
                        `pull_request\.head\.repo\.default_branch).*`)


        if strings.Contains(variable, "github.head_ref") {
                return true
        }
        return strings.Contains(variable, "github.event.") && untrustedContextPattern.MatchString(variable)
}
```
And I can point that it isn't able to detect the following inputs, for example:
- `${{ github.event.issue_comment.comment.body }}`, described in [github's doc](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#issue_comment)
- `${{ github.event.commit_comment.comment.body }}`, described in [github's doc](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#commit_comment)
- `${{ github.event.fork.forkee.name }}` 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
As Dangerous Workflow is a very important check, Scorecard should be able to identify as many Script Injection risks as possible.

We should study more types of [GitHub Events, their payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#about-webhook-events-and-payloads), and make Scorecard as reliable as possible to identify different ways that Script Injections could take place.

**Additional context**
I'd be happy to complete my search and also raise a PR to fix this, but I won't be able to do this in a near future. However, I'm marking this as "Good First issue", as the biggest effort to solve this would be actually a research on GitHub's API. The changes on Scorecard would be simple.

items.title: Integrate workflow security scanning into generated workflow validation
items.body:
## Problem

Fullsend generates GitHub Actions workflows programmatically — the shim workflow (`internal/layers/enrollment.go`) and agent dispatch workflow (`internal/layers/workflows.go`) are Go string constants that get written to target repos and `.fullsend` during `admin install`. These generated workflows are security-critical: they handle secrets, cross-repo dispatch, and agent execution.

Currently, actionlint runs as a pre-commit hook on standalone `.github/workflows/*.yml` files, but it does **not** validate the workflow YAML embedded in Go string constants. A syntax error, expression injection, or permission misconfiguration in these templates would not be caught until the workflow is deployed to a live repo.

## Proposal

Add workflow security scanning at three layers:

### 1. Go test-time validation (actionlint as Go library)

actionlint is already used in pre-commit and is importable as `github.com/rhysd/actionlint`. Add a test that parses and lints all generated workflow string constants:

```go
// internal/layers/workflows_lint_test.go
func TestGeneratedWorkflows_Lint(t *testing.T) {
    workflows := map[string]string{
        "agent.yaml":   agentWorkflowContent,
        "fullsend.yaml": (&EnrollmentLayer{org: "test-org"}).shimWorkflowContent(),
    }
    for name, content := range workflows {
        l, err := actionlint.NewLinter(io.Discard, &actionlint.LinterOptions{})
        require.NoError(t, err)
        errs, err := l.Lint(name, []byte(content), nil)
        require.NoError(t, err)
        assert.Empty(t, errs, "generated workflow %s has lint errors", name)
    }
}
```

This catches syntax errors, type mismatches, invalid action inputs, and script injection at `go test` time — before any deployment.

### 2. Security-focused scanning in CI (zizmor or fluxgate)

actionlint's only security check is script injection detection. Security-specific scanners catch vulnerability classes actionlint does not:

| Vulnerability | actionlint | [zizmor](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) | [fluxgate](https://github.com/north-echo/fluxgate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expression injection | Yes (`expression`) | Yes (`template-injection`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-002) |
| Pwn request | No | Partial (`dangerous-triggers` flags trigger, no execution analysis) | Yes (FG-001, with post-checkout execution + mitigation analysis) |
| Unpinned actions | No | Yes (`unpinned-uses`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-003) |
| Overly broad permissions | No (syntax only) | Yes (`excessive-permissions`) | Yes (FG-004) |
| Cache poisoning | No | Yes (`cache-poisoning`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-010) |
| Self-hosted + external triggers | No | Yes (`self-hosted-runner`) | Yes (FG-009) |
| OIDC misconfiguration | No | No | Yes (FG-008) |
| Bot actor TOCTOU | No | Yes (`bot-conditions`, auto-fix) | Yes (FG-011) |
| Known vulnerable actions | No | Yes (`known-vulnerable-actions`, auto-fix) | No |
| Credential persistence in artifacts | No | Yes (`artipacked`, auto-fix) | No |
| `contains()` substring bypass | No | Yes (`unsound-contains`) | No |
| GITHUB_ENV/PATH writes | No | Yes (`github-env`) | No |
| Secrets in logs | No | Yes (`unredacted-secrets`) | Yes (FG-005) |

**Candidates:**

- **[zizmor](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor)** (Rust, 4k stars, Trail of Bits) — 34 rules, auto-fix for 14, SARIF/JSON/GitHub output. Gold standard for GHA security scanning. Deployed by Grafana Labs across 2,000+ repos. CLI integration from Go via subprocess.
- **[fluxgate](https://github.com/north-echo/fluxgate)** (Go, very new) — 19 rules across GHA/GitLab/Azure. Strongest pwn request detection (post-checkout execution analysis with mitigation modeling). Built in response to the hackerbot-claw campaign. CLI integration only (packages under `internal/`, not importable as Go library).

Add a CI step that extracts generated workflow YAML and scans it:

```yaml
- name: Scan generated workflows
  run: |
    go test -run TestExtractWorkflows ./internal/layers/ -extract-dir /tmp/workflows
    zizmor --format sarif /tmp/workflows/
```

### 3. `workflow_dispatch` input injection (branch `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6`)

The unmerged `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6` branch switches from `workflow_call` to `workflow_dispatch`. The shim in target repos dispatches to `.fullsend` via `gh workflow run`, passing event data as `workflow_dispatch` inputs. This introduces a distinct attack surface:

The v6 shim passes `toJSON(github.event)` as the `event_payload` input, which includes user-supplied content (issue bodies, PR titles, comment text). If the receiving `agent.yaml` interpolates these inputs into `run:` blocks via `${{ inputs.event_payload }}`, it is vulnerable to expression injection — the same class as `${{ github.event.issue.body }}` but arriving through a different path.

**Scanner coverage for `workflow_dispatch` input injection:**

| Tool | Detects dispatch input injection? | Details |
|---|---|---|
| actionlint | Yes | Flags untrusted `${{ }}` expressions in `run:` blocks, including `inputs.*` |
| zizmor (`template-injection`) | Yes | Covers `workflow_dispatch` inputs as injection sinks |
| fluxgate (FG-002) | Yes | Explicitly covers dispatch inputs and reusable workflow inputs |

All three scanners would catch `${{ inputs.event_payload }}` in a `run:` block. However, setting it as an **env var** (`EVENT_PAYLOAD: ${{ inputs.event_payload }}`) is treated differently — the value is passed through the runner's environment, not shell-interpolated, so it is not directly injectable via shell metacharacters. The risk shifts to how downstream code reads and uses that env var.

**Mitigation:** Pass only structured reference fields (repo name, issue number, event type) instead of raw event payloads. The agent fetches full context via the GitHub API using its own App credentials at runtime.

### 4. Runtime protection in generated workflows (Harden-Runner)

Inject [step-security/harden-runner](https://github.com/step-security/harden-runner) as the first step in all generated agent dispatch workflows. This provides runtime monitoring (network egress, file integrity, process activity) that catches supply chain compromise and credential exfiltration during execution — things static analysis cannot detect.

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: step-security/harden-runner@<pinned-sha>
    with:
      egress-policy: audit
```

Harden-Runner has detected real-world supply chain attacks including tj-actions/changed-files (CVE-2025-30066), NX build system, and the hackerbot-claw campaign in CNCF Backstage.

## Why this matters for fullsend specifically

Fullsend generates workflows that:
- Pass secrets cross-repo (App PEM keys via `workflow_call`)
- Handle user-supplied event data (issue bodies, PR descriptions, comments)
- Run on repos the fullsend operator does not control (enrolled target repos)
- Will eventually execute LLM-driven agents with write access to production repos

A vulnerability in a generated workflow template affects **every enrolled repo** simultaneously — the blast radius is the entire fullsend installation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] actionlint Go library validates all generated workflow string constants in `go test`
- [ ] CI pipeline includes security-focused scanning (zizmor or fluxgate) on generated workflows
- [ ] Generated agent dispatch workflows include Harden-Runner as first step
- [ ] Action references in generated workflows use SHA pinning (not mutable tags like `@v4`)
- [ ] Generated workflows set minimum required `permissions:` (not defaults)
- [ ] `workflow_dispatch` inputs (if adopted from `agent-admin-cli-clean-room-v6`) pass only structured reference fields, not raw event payloads

## References

- [Unpacking Security Scanners for GitHub Actions Workflows](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.14455v1) — no single scanner covers all vulnerability classes
- [GitHub Security Lab: Preventing pwn requests](https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/)
- [Upwind: hackerbot-claw campaign](https://www.upwind.io/feed/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-pull-request-rce) — autonomous bot exploiting `pull_request_target` at scale

- Story 6: Prompt Injection Defense (#129)

items.title: Harden GitHub Actions workflows against CI/CD supply chain attacks
items.body:
## Context

A recent automated attack campaign ([hackerbot-claw](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/hackerbot-claw-github-actions-exploitation)) targeted CI/CD pipelines across major open source repositories (Microsoft, DataDog, CNCF projects), achieving remote code execution in multiple targets and exfiltrating a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions from one repository with 140k+ stars.

I audited Evidently's GitHub Actions workflows against the specific attack vectors used in this campaign. **No signs of compromise were found**, but several hardening opportunities exist.

I'd be happy to open a PR for these fixes, but since some changes (particularly adopting Zizmor) would affect your CI/CD process, I thought it best to open an issue for discussion first.

## Findings

### 1. Script Injection via `${{ }}` in `run:` blocks (Medium-High)

Several workflows interpolate user-controlled values directly into shell commands, which enables [script injection](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#understanding-the-risk-of-script-injections). An attacker can craft a branch name containing shell metacharacters to execute arbitrary commands.

**Affected locations:**

| File | Lines | Expression | Notes |
|------|-------|-----------|-------|
| `main.yml` | 172, 384, 441 | `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}` in shell | Branch name → shell injection |
| `main.yml` | 274 | `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}` as CLI arg | Branch name → argument injection |
| `main.yml` | 78, 84, 90, 96-97 | `${{ steps.changed-files.outputs.*_files }}` in echo | Filenames from PR → shell injection |
| `deploy-artifacts-to-github-pages.yml` | 70 | `${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_branch }}` in shell | **Most concerning** — `workflow_run` runs with base repo's full write permissions and secrets |
| `docker.yml` | 16 | `echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PWD }}` | Secret expanded inline in shell |

**Fix:** Assign `${{ }}` values to environment variables, then reference them as `"$VAR"` in shell. Environment variables are treated as data, not code:

```yaml
# Before (vulnerable):
run: |
  BRANCH_NAME="${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}"

# After (safe):
env:
  BRANCH_NAME: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}
run: |
  BRANCH_NAME="${BRANCH_NAME//\//-}"
```

### 2. Missing Top-Level `permissions:` (Medium)

`main.yml`, `docker.yml`, and `examples.yml` don't set a top-level `permissions:` key, so the `GITHUB_TOKEN` gets the repository default (typically `write-all`).

**Fix:** Add `permissions: read-all` at the workflow level and grant specific write permissions only to jobs that need them. `release.yml` already does this correctly per-job.

### 3. Unpinned Actions (Medium)

All actions use mutable tag references (`@v4`, `@v5`) rather than immutable SHA pins. If a third-party action's repository is compromised, a force-pushed tag would run malicious code in your CI.

Notable concerns:
- **`actions/checkout@master`** in `docker.yml` — tracks a *branch*, not even a tag
- **`tj-actions/changed-files@v42`** — this third-party action was the subject of a [real supply chain attack in March 2025](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/tj-actions-changed-files-attack-detection) where it was backdoored to exfiltrate CI secrets

**Recommendation:** Adopt [**Zizmor**](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) ([docs](https://docs.zizmor.sh/)) — a static analysis tool purpose-built for GitHub Actions security. It can:
- Detect all of the above issues (script injection, unpinned actions, permission problems)
- Run as a [GitHub Action in CI](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-action) to catch regressions
- Help generate SHA-pinned action references

You can also use Dependabot or Renovate to keep SHA-pinned actions up to date automatically.

### 4. Docker Secret Handling (Low)

`docker.yml` uses inline secret expansion for Docker login:
```yaml
run: echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PWD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_LOGIN }} --password-stdin
```

`release.yml` already uses `docker/login-action@v3` for this — the manual workflow should do the same.

## Summary

| Issue | Severity | Effort |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Script injection in `deploy-artifacts-to-github-pages.yml` | Medium-High | Low (env var refactor) |
| Script injection in `main.yml` | Medium | Low (env var refactor) |
| Missing `permissions: read-all` | Medium | Low (add one line per workflow) |
| Unpinned actions (especially `tj-actions/changed-files`) | Medium | Medium (adopt Zizmor + Dependabot) |
| `actions/checkout@master` in `docker.yml` | Medium | Trivial |
| Docker secret handling in `docker.yml` | Low | Low (use `docker/login-action`) |

Happy to submit a PR for some or all of these if that would be helpful — just let me know which changes you'd prefer to handle internally.

- `claude.yml` already has `author_association` checks (MEMBER/OWNER/COLLABORATOR)
- `ci.yml` already has `permissions: contents: read`

## Remaining recommendation

Set org-level default token permissions to read-only in GitHub Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions.

## Test plan

- [ ] CI passes on this PR (validates pinned SHAs resolve correctly)
- [ ] Trigger `@claude` on a test PR to verify allowedTools doesn't break normal usage
- [ ] Verify CODEOWNERS shows up in branch protection rules

Several skills pin versions below published security fixes, misquote advisory ranges or severities, or carry routine stale pins. Found in a full collection audit plus an independent review (2026-09-24/25).

Security floors:
- frontend-design: Next.js 16.3.4 is inside `>=16.2.0 <16.3.6` of GHSA-vcvr-r3jv-pc5j (2026-09-22). Needs 16.3.6.
- ci-cd: GitLab 19.3.1 predates the 2026-09-23 critical patch (19.4.1 / 19.3.3 / 19.2.7).
- networking: Unbound 1.26.0 -> 1.26.1, strongSwan 6.0.7 -> 6.1.0, Traefik 3.7.12 -> 3.7.13, HAProxy 3.4.4 -> 3.4.5, cloudflared 2026.8.3 -> 2026.9.3.
- synology-dsm: DSM 7.3 floor needs 7.3.2-86009-4 (SA-26:13).
- databases: MongoDB 8.0.30 -> 8.0.32 (CVE-2026-89099); CVE-2026-2005 floor misses the 15.16 / 14.21 lanes.
- observability: Grafana 13.2.1 -> 13.2.2, Loki 3.7.7 -> 3.7.8.
- mcp: TS SDK 2.1.0 / legacy 1.30.1 hardening; Python SDK CVE-2026-59950 missing.

Advisory accuracy:
- docker: go-archive range is `< 0.3.0`, not `< 0.2.2`; the "4.66.1 floor" line contradicts the table.
- ci-cd supply-chain reference: harden-runner latest is v2.21.0; DCT is scheduled for retirement 2026-12-08, not retired; HackerBot-Claw target list is wrong; SLSA current spec is v1.2; unsourced slopsquatting stats.
- security-audit: Semgrep 1.178.0, TruffleHog 3.97.9; OWASP Top 10:2025 date wording.
- git: CVE-2026-62960 fixed-version note, GitLab 17.x fixed versions; fj 0.6.0 hedge is outdated.
- rhel-fedora, debian-ubuntu: CVE-2026-46300 called "exploited"; only a public PoC exists.
- ansible: CVE-2024-11079 severity is Low.

Routine pins: Forgejo v16.0.5 / v15.0.9, Gitea Runner (renamed, v4.0.0), Woodpecker 3.18.1, OPNsense 26.7.4_1, React 19.3.0, gh 2.101.0, glab 1.119.0, MariaDB 11.8.9, bpg/proxmox 0.113.1, Packer 1.16.1, OTel Collector 0.161.0, Alertmanager 0.34.1, Docker Engine 29.8.1, Syft 1.52.0, Podman 6.1.2, Vitest 5.0.1, k6 2.3.0, cargo-nextest 0.9.146, LLM SDK pins, Redis/Valkey pins, networking internal pin drift (Headscale, OpenVPN, Traefik).

Expected: pins match current releases with sources, security floors match the advisories.

items.title: Pin rustpython #8733 and consume host_env APIs
items.body:
## Summary

Pins every rustpython crate to `youknowone/RustPython` `3fde5cac` ([RustPython#8733](https://github.com/RustPython/RustPython/pull/8733)), which sits on `#8728` (`wait3`/`wait4`) and `#8730` (`pread`/`pwrite`).

Consumes the host_env surface that used to be copied locally:

- `nt::symlink` for the MAX_PATH `_check_dirW` probe
- `winapi::version_ex_triple` for `sys.getwindowsversion`
- `nt::set_file_times` for Windows `os.utime`
- `socket::uuid_from_string_w` / `uuid_to_string_w` for AF_HYPERV GUIDs
- `posix::pread` / `pwrite` / `wait3` / `wait4` (`interp_posix.pread`/`pwrite`, `app_posix.wait3`/`wait4`)

Drops the now-unused `windows-sys` `System_Rpc` and `System_SystemInformation` features.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo check -p pyre-interpreter --features dynasm` (macOS; unix pread/pwrite/wait3/wait4)
- [ ] CI Windows (symlink / getwindowsversion / utime / UUID)

items.title: Security: pr-quality-check.yaml workflow is vulnerable to code execution and token theft from fork PRs
items.body:
## Summary

Your `pr-quality-check.yaml` workflow is vulnerable to the classic ["Pwn Request"](https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/) pattern — it uses `pull_request_target` to check out and execute untrusted fork code with `contents: write` and `pull-requests: write` permissions. This was recently exploited by an automated bot that achieved remote code execution and **exfiltrated the GITHUB_TOKEN** from this repository.

Between February 28, 2026, the `hackerbot-claw` bot opened 6 pull requests against this repository ([#6058](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6058), [#6059](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6059), [#6060](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6060), [#6061](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6061), [#6068](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6068), [#6069](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/pull/6069)). 

## Recommended fixes

1. **Switch from `pull_request_target` to `pull_request`** — Fork PRs won't have access to secrets with `pull_request`. This is the simplest and safest fix.

items.title: Detect action-form agent shell and update whitepaper
items.body:
Extends the fork-triggerable shell-exec rule to catch the action form of claude-code-action, not just CLI invocations. This closes the gap that the Cline compromise fell through: an agent granted Bash or Edit/Write tools reaches code execution on the runner even when the job holds only contents: read. The severity split is preserved, so a job with provable repo write stays with the critical rule and does not double-report.

Whitepaper changes:
- Add a remediation follow-up section reporting that 26 percent of the original findings no longer flag after a re-scan.
- Add the Cline and Hackerbot-Claw incidents and frame the primitive as the agent variant of poisoned pipeline execution.
- Add a references section with verified source locators.
